title: Session fixation and privilege transitions without token rotation
summary: Session fixation becomes plausible when a session identifier that existed before authentication remains valid afterwards, so a token an attacker planted or observed inherits the victim's authenticated state. Verification must establish where the token is issued, whether the server accepts a client-supplied identifier, whether a new identifier is minted at every privilege transition, and whether the pre-authentication token is genuinely invalidated on the server rather than only replaced in the browser.
detection_signals: The identifier present before login is still accepted after login, or the framework's session regeneration call is absent from the authentication handler.
The application accepts a session identifier from a URL parameter, form field, or arbitrary client-set cookie instead of issuing every identifier itself.
Privilege transitions other than the initial login, such as step-up authentication, impersonation, tenant switching, or account linking, do not mint a new session identifier.
safe_local_tests: Against a local instance, capture the pre-authentication identifier, complete a fixture login in the same client, and assert that the old identifier is rejected while the new one works.
Attempt to set a session identifier from the client and confirm the server issues its own value instead of adopting the supplied one.
Record the identifier before and after each privilege transition, the server-side invalidation outcome for the old value, and the cookie attributes in force, using fixture accounts only.
false_positive_traps: A cookie value that looks unchanged may be an opaque wrapper around a rotated server-side session, so the server's acceptance of the old identifier is what decides the finding.
A stateless token architecture can rotate identity through a new signed token and a revoked reference token, and calling that fixation without checking revocation is a misdiagnosis.
Cookie flags such as Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite reduce planting opportunities but do not substitute for rotation, and their presence alone does not clear the defect.
remediation_patterns: Mint a new session identifier at authentication and at every privilege transition, and invalidate the previous server-side session in the same operation.
Never accept a session identifier from request-controlled locations, and issue every identifier from a cryptographically secure generator with sufficient entropy.
Bind session termination to logout, password or factor change, and administrative revocation, so an inherited or stolen identifier can be retired everywhere it is accepted.
regression_proof: A test proves the pre-authentication identifier is rejected after login while the newly issued identifier authorizes the same request.
Coverage includes step-up authentication and other privilege transitions plus logout revocation, so a handler that stops regenerating the session fails the suite.
